episodes.title: Expulsion of C. A. Buchanan from West Point, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The expulsion of C. A. Buchanan from West Point, Mississippi, took place in August 1904, when a mob organized at a white mass meeting ordered the Black editor and preacher to close his newspaper office and leave the state. Buchanan moved his paper to Guthrie, Oklahoma, and recounted the episode there in an editorial a year later.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Hall
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ed Hall took place near Charlotte, North Carolina, in late July 1905, when about a hundred men hunted Hall, a young Black man accused of attempting to assault a farmer's wife, and there was talk of lynching him. He was arrested at Pineville the same afternoon and jailed, the talk subsided, and in August he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to seven years at hard labor.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Gadsden, Alabama (1905)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Gadsden, Alabama, took place on a Sunday night in late July 1905, when a mob of about 300 people marched on the Gadsden jail to seize six Black prisoners charged with the rape and murder of a white widow, Mrs. S. J. Smith. The mob dispersed after a congressman, the militia commander and the sheriff appealed to it.

episodes.title: Shooting of a Black farm laborer and his son near Savannah (1905)
episodes.lead: The shooting of a Black farm laborer and his son near Savannah was an attack in the summer of 1905 in which a white man, in a county near Savannah, shot down a colored man and one of his sons after the man refused to work faster in the heat. A second son escaped by running for his life, and the white man was not molested. The case is known only from an editorial in the Savannah Tribune, which cited it as an example of the treatment that drove Black workers from the farms.

episodes.title: Lynching of Will Harris
episodes.lead: The lynching of Will Harris was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a mob of about fifty men who took him from officers aboard a Yazoo and Mississippi Valley train at Black Bayou, near Glendora, Mississippi, in late July 1905. Harris was accused, with his brother, of shooting two white men near Sharkey, and white newspapers from Mississippi to Wisconsin carried the hanging as a short news item. A Greenwood dispatch singled out one detail: members of the mob handed the deputy sheriff back his handcuffs and told him they were no longer needed.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Andrew Dinwiddie
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Andrew Dinwiddie took place at Paris, Texas, on August 17, 1905, when a mob took Dinwiddie, a Black man accused of trying to assault a white girl, from officers and prepared to hang him in the public square. County Judge Love talked the crowd into returning him to the sheriff, and three days later a grand jury declined to indict him and he was released. The wire story of a mob turned back by a judge's speech ran across the South, and Texas editors later pointed to the case as a near-lynching of an innocent man.

episodes.title: Attempted hanging of Andrew Holbrook
episodes.lead: The attempted hanging of Andrew Holbrook took place in Newport News, Virginia, on the night of August 28, 1905, when grocer Frank L. Townsend and members of his household bound Holbrook, a Black man, and tied a rope around his neck. Spectators drawn by his cries persuaded Townsend to stop, and police took Holbrook away; he was later jailed for six months for trying to break into Townsend's lunch wagon. Wire versions of the story ran in papers as far away as Illinois and Kentucky under headlines such as "Negro Saved From Lynching."

episodes.title: Assault on Arthur Glande
episodes.lead: The assault on Arthur Glande was the beating of a Black man at Grand Bay, Alabama, in late August 1905, which he said was carried out by two young white men, August Fichet and Ashton Page, with persimmon limbs. The two men were charged with assault and released on bond, and a Mobile correspondent of the Montgomery Advertiser described the episode as "a peculiar story" because it grew out of a quarrel over race and kinship.

episodes.title: Congress saloon fight between Patrolman Flannigan and Joe Baskerville
episodes.lead: The Congress saloon fight between Patrolman Flannigan and Joe Baskerville was a brawl in Seattle, Washington, early on Friday, August 11, 1905, in which a police officer threatened to shoot a Black porter and was beaten unconscious by him. Both men were arrested, and the Seattle Star later counted the officer among four patrolmen 'victims' of that week.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bees
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bees was the killing of a Black man by a mob near the Leake plantation at Rosetta, Mississippi, at the end of August or on September 1, 1905. He was charged with an attempted criminal assault on a white girl, and the news reached papers across the country only as brief wire items. The single Black-press notice found was one sentence in a weekly news digest.

episodes.title: Killing of Ben Scott
episodes.lead: The killing of Ben Scott was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable Meek and Deputy Hanes during an attempted arrest at his home eight miles north of Mount Pleasant, Texas, on the night of 19 August 1905. Scott surrendered after he was wounded and died in the county jail the next night. The only report found, a Mount Pleasant dispatch, gave the officers' account that he had fired first.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of Bill Pierce
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of Bill Pierce was the night beating of William (Bill) Pierce, a Black resident of Lake Park, Georgia, by a party of white men on August 7, 1905, after he refused an order to leave the community. Pierce swore out warrants against five men described as prominent citizens, among them a justice of the peace and a merchant whose whiskey case he was to testify in, and they were placed under bond for superior court.

episodes.title: Killing of Ike Kinney
episodes.lead: The killing of Ike Kinney was the shooting of a Black man, Ike or Isaac Kinney, by a posse of citizens at Doella, six miles south of Lewisville, Arkansas, on August 3, 1905. Kinney was hunted as the accused killer of a Black man at Stamps and of E. R. Ferguson, a railroad claim agent with a pursuing posse, and was reported to have wounded four more people before he was shot. An Arkansas Gazette dispatch listing his "bloody record" ran in white papers across the country, and one Black weekly, the St. Louis Palladium, reprinted it.

episodes.title: Posse shooting of Bob Jones
episodes.lead: The posse shooting of Bob Jones took place at about midnight on August 11, 1905, in Monroe, Louisiana, when a posse shot and dangerously wounded Jones, a Black brakeman on the Iron Mountain Railroad. Jones was accused of assaulting a conductor of the railroad, and his chances of recovery were reported to be small.

episodes.title: Simmons gang threat against Boley
episodes.lead: The Simmons gang threat against Boley was a reported threat in August 1905 by the outlaw Andy Simmons to attack Boley, Oklahoma, a Black town, and kill its Black officials and residents in revenge for his brother's death and his brothers' arrests. Extra police and marshals guarded the town, and many Black residents of Boley and nearby Paden were said to be leaving their homes. No attack was reported, and the threat appeared only in the Guthrie Daily Leader.

episodes.title: Dynamiting of the Black Baptist church at Carlisle, Indiana
episodes.lead: The dynamiting of the Black Baptist church at Carlisle, Indiana, took place early on August 25, 1905, when dynamite placed under the altar destroyed the building. Dispatches from Vincennes described it as the result of a "race war" in the town and reported threats that every Black resident would be driven out if anyone was arrested. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and several Southern editors cited it to accuse Northern papers of ignoring violence outside the South.

episodes.title: Police pursuit and clubbing of Cassius Coolidge
episodes.lead: The police pursuit and clubbing of Cassius Coolidge took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the evening of August 25, 1905, when policemen fired on Coolidge, a Black porter, during a four-block chase and clubbed him after his capture. Coolidge had just shot two Black men, Oscar and Harry Grimes, killing Oscar; the St. Louis Republic, the only paper found to report it, treated the episode as a shooting story.

episodes.title: Lynching of Cleveland McBee
episodes.lead: The lynching of Cleveland McBee was the hanging and shooting of a Black youth by a mob at Cedar Bluff, Mississippi, in late August 1905. McBee was accused of assaulting the twelve-year-old daughter of a farmer on whose place he lived, and the mob cut the railroad wires so that the Governor would not learn of the killing. The only report found is a front-page story in the Columbus Dispatch, which presented the hanging as a deserved penalty.

episodes.title: Luna Park restaurant riot
episodes.lead: The Luna Park restaurant riot was a fight at the Cafe Neapolitan in Luna Park, Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, on the evening of August 22, 1905, that began when waiters refused to serve Charles Julius Miller, a Black visitor from Chicago, and grew into what the dispatch called a "desperate race riot" of about two hundred people. Miller was seriously injured, several others were sent to hospitals, and between fifteen and about fifty people were arrested. A single wire dispatch carried the story to white and Black papers from New York to Washington State.

episodes.title: Peonage case of Charlie Warren
episodes.lead: The peonage case of Charlie Warren was a federal prosecution begun in August 1905, when J. K. Mitchell, a farmer of Wilcox County, Georgia, was arrested on a charge of holding Warren, a fifteen-year-old Black boy, in servitude. Mitchell was jailed at Macon to await a hearing, and the arrest was carried as a brief wire item by papers from Maine to Virginia.

episodes.title: Newark crowd attack on Clarence Spain and Mary Stein
episodes.lead: The Newark crowd attack on Clarence Spain and Mary Stein took place in Newark, New Jersey, in early August 1905, when a street crowd set upon a Black man and his white bride as they left the justice of the peace's office where they had just married. No injuries were reported and the couple got away, but papers in New York and Denver carried the story.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Oscar Bates
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Oscar Bates took place at the Good Times Inn in Comfort, Texas, on or shortly before August 20, 1905, when armed German citizens came for Bates, a Black dishwasher accused of insulting a local girl. Bates escaped under gunfire, and the inn's Black staff then left Comfort for San Antonio, leaving the town without Black residents.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Dan Howard
episodes.lead: The police shooting of Dan Howard took place in Birmingham, Alabama, about 11:30 p.m. on 16 August 1905, when Policeman Ray shot Howard, a Black man, as he ran from arrest. Howard was wounded in the abdomen and first reported likely to die, but a day later physicians said he had a chance to recover.

episodes.title: Bradley mill posse shooting
episodes.lead: The Bradley mill posse shooting was a pursuit and exchange of gunfire between a Mobile County sheriff's posse and a group of Black sawmill workers from Bradley, Alabama, on August 25-27, 1905. Officers said they fired on the men at Beaver Meadow after the men fired first, and a deputy believed he had hit one of them, though no wounded man was found. One man, Boston Moore, was jailed, and the man the Montgomery Advertiser called the ringleader, Dave Wells, was last reported hiding in a swamp.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Dr. Howard from Hattiesburg
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Dr. Howard from Hattiesburg was an order, reported in late August 1905, that a Black physician leave Hattiesburg, Mississippi. The only known account, a brief editorial note in the Oklahoma Safeguard, does not say who gave the order or whether he left. The paper treated the case as an example of the "move-on" orders it said were given to Black men who prospered in the South.

episodes.title: Pembroke armed posse after the shooting of a brakeman (1905)
episodes.lead: The Pembroke armed posse of August 1905 was a turnout of about 25 armed citizens of Pembroke, Kentucky, on 17 August 1905, after a Black man riding a freight train shot a white brakeman near Casky. A posse led by the town marshal arrested four Black men, although the brakeman said none of them had shot him. The Hopkinsville Kentuckian said the citizens were "out for gore."

episodes.title: Paradise Alley race riot, Elkton, 1905
episodes.lead: The Paradise Alley race riot was a fight between white and Black people in the Paradise alley section of Elkton, Maryland, late on a Saturday night in early August 1905. Pistols and knives were used, several people were badly cut, and seven people were eventually arrested. It is known only from two brief notes in one Eastern Shore weekly, which called it a "race riot."

episodes.title: Lynching at Eros, Louisiana (1905)
episodes.lead: The lynching at Eros, Louisiana, was the reported killing in August 1905 of an unnamed Black man accused of being one of two men who shot and wounded J. H. Sanders, a merchant who was serving as a quarantine guard at Eros. According to a Monroe dispatch, he was lynched on the night of August 11, and the second accused man was to be lynched as soon as he was caught. The story reached readers only as a brief wire item in white newspapers from Washington to Michigan, and no follow-up was found.

episodes.title: Burning of a Black church and schoolhouse in De Soto County, 1905
episodes.lead: The burning of a Black church and schoolhouse in De Soto County took place in late August 1905, when a masked band of "whitecappers" set fire to a "negro church and schoolhouse" and burned both to the ground. No one was identified, and the only known report is a short item in the Macon Beacon of Macon, Mississippi.

episodes.title: Beating of a Black youth during a chase near St. Asaph, Virginia
episodes.lead: The beating of a Black youth near St. Asaph, Virginia, took place on August 22, 1905, when Mr. McDonald and other residents of Alexandria county chased down four 'colored youths' and one who resisted was badly beaten in the face. All four were jailed on a charge of abusive language and disorderly conduct, and a rumor that a criminal assault had been attempted was denied at the courthouse.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Francis Smith
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Francis Smith took place near Franklin Park, New Jersey, on August 5, 1905, when a posse hunting Smith, a Black farm hand, found him in a barn and nearly lynched him. Smith had been accused of trying to assault his employer's fifteen-year-old daughter the night before. A Somerville policeman brought him before a justice, who held him for the grand jury, and a Hoboken editorial later held up the case as evidence that Northerners too were roused by such accusations.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of George Davis
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of George Davis was an attack on a Black mail carrier on the route between Bogue Chitto and Ambler, Mississippi, whose house was fired into by white men who threatened to kill him unless he quit carrying the mail, as reported in 1905. A federal grand jury indicted four men, and two of them, Douglass Holloway and John Ratliff, were brought in by United States marshals and released on bond.

episodes.title: Police beating of George Sewell
episodes.lead: The police beating of George Sewell took place on the night of Sunday, August 6, 1905, when Patrolman Patrick J. Carmody, off duty and in plain clothes, beat Sewell, a young Black man, with his revolver while arresting him on West 28th Street in New York City. Magistrate Pool of the West Side court discharged Sewell and held the policeman in $1,000 bail for felonious assault, saying he had struck Sewell because he was Black.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Williams
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Williams took place at McRae, Georgia, on the night of August 18, 1905, when a crowd of 75 to 100 men gathered to lynch Williams, a Black prisoner charged with an attempted assault upon a white woman. Sheriff Dowdy had learned of the plan and moved Williams to the jail at Macon, and no violence against him was reported. Papers outside Georgia carried the story as a brief Associated Press item crediting the sheriff with defeating the mob.

episodes.title: Burning of Henry Jenkins's house
episodes.lead: The burning of Henry Jenkins's house was a fire, believed to have been set, that destroyed the home of a Black carpenter just outside Newport News, Virginia, on the night of August 5, 1905. Jenkins, his wife and four children escaped, and he told the local paper that several people had threatened to burn the house.

episodes.title: William Strickland peonage case
episodes.lead: The William Strickland peonage case was a federal prosecution in August 1905 of William Strickland, a Black farmer at Baconton, Georgia, accused of holding a Black boy, Henry Sterling, in involuntary servitude. Strickland was arrested by a deputy U.S. marshal, held on bond, and reportedly bound over to the federal grand jury. Papers treated the case as notable because the peonage law was being used against a Black employer, which a Macon dispatch called a first for the federal courts there.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Young
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Young was the hanging of a Black tenant by a mob of about 100 men on the Bass plantation near Lake Cormorant, DeSoto County, Mississippi, on the night of August 16, 1905. Young, accused of killing the white plantation manager Edward E. Perry on Sunday, August 13, was taken from Sheriff Withers and a deputy at a railroad station. A Memphis account called the hanging quiet and orderly and said Black onlookers approved; the Oklahoma Safeguard, a Black paper, reprinted it and answered it in an editorial.

episodes.title: Killing of Ike Kinney
episodes.lead: The killing of Ike Kinney took place on August 3, 1905, when a posse of citizens shot Kinney, a Black man, dead in a river bottom at Doella, a plantation post office six miles south of Lewisville, Arkansas. Kinney had been hunted for about a day after he was accused of killing a Black man at Stamps and then shooting E. R. Ferguson, a railroad claim agent riding with a posse. A wire special from Lewisville listing his 'bloody record' of two killings and four woundings ran in dozens of papers, including the Black weekly St. Louis Palladium.

episodes.title: Killing of Jessie Jones
episodes.lead: The killing of Jessie Jones was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Jessie Jones by T. B. Murray, the marshal of a town printed as "Dlo," apparently in Mississippi, in or shortly before August 1905. The only account found, a single sentence in The Leader of Brookhaven, Mississippi, said Jones was killed "while resisting arrest."

episodes.title: Beating and expulsion of Jim Cherry
episodes.lead: The beating and expulsion of Jim Cherry took place at Sulphur Springs, Texas, in August 1905, when citizens beat Cherry, a Black man, over a remark about a young white woman and ordered him out of town. According to the wire account, the citizens first debated whether to lynch him, and he left town in a covered wagon. The incident was reported as an aftermath of the burning of Tom Williams at Sulphur Springs, in which the same woman was the alleged victim.

episodes.title: Flogging of Jim Lawyer
episodes.lead: The flogging of Jim Lawyer took place on the night of August 9, 1905, when about twenty men took Lawyer, a Black man, from a house near Bruceville, Texas, and whipped him. According to the only account, a Waco dispatch, he was punished for condemning the whites for the lynching of Sank Majors and was told to leave the area, which he did the next morning.

episodes.title: Killing of John Hill
episodes.lead: The killing of John Hill was the fatal shooting of a Black passenger by Deputy Sheriff J. P. Brents on a Southern Railway passenger train near Coalburg, Alabama, on the night of 14 August 1905. The deputy said Hill had twice reached toward his pocket while being arrested, and officers called the shooting self-defense.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Moore
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Moore took place early on Sunday, August 27, 1905, when a masked crowd took Moore, a young Black man, from the Craven County jail at New Bern, North Carolina, hanged him from the Neuse River bridge and riddled his body with bullets. Moore had been accused two days earlier of striking a white storekeeper's wife with a meat axe during an attempted robbery. Papers across the country blamed the lynching on the $300 bond set at his hearing, and Governor Glenn ordered the lynchers prosecuted.

episodes.title: Peonage arrests of the Young brothers in Lafayette County, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The peonage arrests of the Young brothers took place in Lafayette County, Mississippi, on August 24, 1905, when federal officers arrested Brigham, Allen and James Young, Lee Rogers and Charles Butts, five white men, on a charge of holding John Ross, a Black man, in bondage. The five gave bond to appear before a United States commissioner on September 5. The local Oxford Eagle called it the first peonage arrest in the county, and the case ran as a short dispatch in papers from New York to Texas.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Lewis and Kid George
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ed Lewis and Kid George was the hanging of two Black men by a mob at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, on the night of August 4, 1905. Both were jailed as accomplices in the killing that morning of J. G. Smith, a white guard over the city convicts, and the mob took them from the jail and hanged them from a bridge. White papers called it an 'orderly' lynching, while a Hattiesburg mass meeting condemned it as 'cowardly murder'.

episodes.title: Knoxville streetcar mob of 1905
episodes.lead: The Knoxville streetcar mob of 1905 was an attack in which a mob tore Black passengers off streetcars on the "Lousdale Line" in Knoxville, Tennessee, soon after the state's "Jim Crow" streetcar law went into effect in the summer of 1905. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the attack is known from a single item in the Indianapolis Freeman, which presented it as the start of a Black boycott of the city's streetcars.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Lemuel Cannon
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Lemuel Cannon was a gathering of more than a hundred men and boys who surrounded the Minneapolis home of Cannon, a Black man accused of assaulting a young girl, on the evening of August 8, 1905, and organized a 'lynching party'. Cannon was in jail at the time, and most of the crowd went home after learning by telephone that he could not get bail. He was later indicted for criminal assault and tried in district court.

episodes.title: Whipping death of Liddell at Sugar Hill camp
episodes.lead: The whipping death of Liddell at Sugar Hill camp was the death in August 1905 of a Black convict at a labor camp in Bartow County, Georgia, after a whipping by the camp's deputy warden, J. W. Tierce. A county coroner's verdict that Liddell had been whipped to death led the state prison commission to suspend Tierce, but State Warden J. C. Moore reported after his own inquiry that the prisoner had died of natural causes. A coroner's jury at Cartersville then held Tierce under $5,000 bond for manslaughter and rebuked Moore, a sequence carried by white papers across the South and by the Savannah Tribune.

episodes.title: Macon quarantine shooting (1905)
episodes.lead: The Macon quarantine shooting took place at noon on Thursday, August 3, 1905, in Macon, Noxubee County, Mississippi, when two men, Sam Irion and a Mr. Maury, fired their pistols at a Black man who had left a railroad car without a health certificate. The man fired back, escaped across a cornfield, and was not found by the sheriff's bloodhounds; the only known report, in the local Macon Beacon, treated it as "An Exciting Incident."

episodes.title: Thomasville posse hunt for Manuel Harty
episodes.lead: The Thomasville posse hunt for Manuel Harty was an armed manhunt near Thomasville, Georgia, in August 1905, in which mounted townsmen followed the sheriff in pursuit of a Black farmhand accused of assaulting a farmer's wife and threatened to lynch him if they caught him. Harty was not reported captured; the posse brought in another Black man, who was released when the woman did not identify him. White papers in Georgia and Florida carried the story under headlines predicting a lynching.

episodes.title: Meansville camp meeting shooting
episodes.lead: The Meansville camp meeting shooting was an exchange of gunfire between white marshals and Black men at a Black camp meeting at Meansville, Georgia, south of Zebulon, reported in a dispatch dated August 23, 1905. One Black man was killed and three others were jailed, among them an Atlanta man charged with selling whisky. The only coverage found is a brief wire item reprinted in two Florida papers.

episodes.title: New Haven posse lynching threat (1905)
episodes.lead: The New Haven posse lynching threat was a reported manhunt in New Haven, Connecticut, on August 14, 1905, in which a posse searched for an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a nineteen-year-old white girl, intending to lynch him once he was caught. The only account found is a brief dispatch printed two days later in a South Carolina weekly, and it gives no outcome.

episodes.title: Harlem police clubbing of August 1905
episodes.lead: The Harlem police clubbing of August 1905 took place on August 8, 1905, near One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street in Harlem, New York City, when police reserves clubbed a crowd of Black people after a policeman was attacked while arresting a Black woman. Three people were arrested and held in the Harlem Court for participating in a riot. The only report found, in the New York Evening World, presented the incident as a "race riot" started by the woman.

episodes.title: Killing of Oliver Lott
episodes.lead: The killing of Oliver Lott took place at Tunnel Springs, Alabama, on August 22, 1905, when a posse of white citizens shot Lott, a Black mill laborer, to death in a house where he had barricaded himself. Lott was accused of shooting two white carpenters, John and Harry Helton, in a quarrel over a debt, and of fatally wounding the posse's leader, the mill owner G. Talley. The Associated Press spread the story nationally as a 'negro murderer' killed by a posse; an Alabama report added that the posse's fire also wounded the house's Black owner.

episodes.title: Manhunt for Phelp Bunyan
episodes.lead: The manhunt for Phelp Bunyan was an armed pursuit of a young Black man in Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, in August 1905, after he was accused of attempting to assault a young white woman. The Montgomery Advertiser headlined the story "LYNCHING IS FEARED," but four days later a man of nearly the same name was reported arrested and jailed at Tuscaloosa, where he denied the charge.

episodes.title: Killing of Pink Hane
episodes.lead: The killing of Pink Hane was the fatal shooting of a Mississippi man by a quarantine guard near Lagrange, Tennessee, on the night of August 13, 1905. He was shot while trying to cross a quarantine line into Tennessee and died several hours later, and a Memphis dispatch described it as the first death from efforts to evade the quarantine in that area.

episodes.title: 1905 New York West Side race riots
episodes.lead: The 1905 New York West Side race riots were clashes between white and Black residents of Manhattan's West Side tenement blocks in the Sixties, near Tenth Avenue, in July 1905, during which police were accused of clubbing Black men while sparing white attackers. Police Commissioner McAdoo transferred the precinct captain and appointed a committee to study the causes of the riots. The Black press made police conduct the central issue, and the riots prompted a Black defense league and demands for an investigation.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Rayville, Louisiana (1905)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Rayville, Louisiana, took place on or shortly before August 4, 1905, when a mob of about 100 armed men took a Black man from a Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific train and prepared to hang him. He was released after the husband of the woman he was accused of slapping said he was innocent; northern papers presented it as lynchers acting on rumor.

episodes.title: 1905 Rockport, Kentucky, clash
episodes.lead: In the 1905 Rockport, Kentucky, clash, fifteen to twenty armed white men fired on a crowd of Black people at Rockport, Ohio County, on Sunday, August 13, 1905. No one was reported seriously hurt; fifteen white men and four Black men were charged.

episodes.title: Police shooting at Roland Jones
episodes.lead: The police shooting at Roland Jones took place on the night of Monday, 21 August 1905, in Virginia, when an officer fired a pistol at Jones, a Black man, to make him stop. Jones was not reported hurt, but a false report that someone had been killed caused a stir, and the next morning he was fined $10 for beating a woman named Laura Brackett.

episodes.title: St. Louis Broadway streetcar shooting
episodes.lead: The St. Louis Broadway streetcar shooting took place at about 1:30 a.m. on 16 August 1905, when a group of young men harassed Clarence (or Charles) Hunt, a Black youth, on a streetcar near Broadway and Olive street in St. Louis, Missouri, and one of them fired a revolver at him. The shots missed Hunt but wounded two other passengers, Sam Edwards, a Black man, and John Rogers. Beverly Brown, whom Edwards and Hunt identified as the gunman, was arrested and denied the charge.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sank Majors
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sank Majors took place at Waco, Texas, early on August 8, 1905, when a large mob broke into the county jail, seized Majors, a young Black prisoner, and hanged him from a bridge over the Brazos River. Majors had been convicted of criminally assaulting a white woman and sentenced to death, but a judge had granted him a new trial three days earlier. Many white editorials blamed the court rather than the mob, and a Black man who criticized the lynching was flogged in the county.

episodes.title: Whipping of Si Liddell and Jones
episodes.lead: The whipping of Si Liddell and Jones was the flogging of two Black men by a crowd near Glory, Texas, in August 1905, after an improvised tribunal convicted them of remarks about a young white woman. Both men were whipped and ordered to leave the community. Papers outside Texas treated the case as a curiosity: one called it a "double lynching" averted by a "Kangaroo Court," while a wire version stressed that Black residents had helped punish the men.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sisco
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sisco took place in Rockland County, New York, on August 20, 1905, when crowds threatened to lynch a Black prisoner named Sisco at Haverstraw and then went to the New City jail intending to hang him. Sisco was held as the suspected companion of a man named Brown, accused of shooting two Haverstraw policemen the night before, and the crowds failed to reach him. Only the New-York Tribune reported the lynching threats in detail; a wire story printed as far away as Nebraska carried the shooting and Sisco's capture without the mob.

episodes.title: Court-ordered whipping of seven Black boys in Taylorsville, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The court-ordered whipping of seven Black boys in Taylorsville, Kentucky, took place in August 1905, when the town's police judge made a public whipping by their parents the condition of their release from jail on charges of disorderly conduct. The boys, aged twelve to eighteen, were whipped one by one before a large crowd under the town marshal's supervision, and the Louisville Courier-Journal's dispatch praised the sentence as "a good example."

episodes.title: Killing of Tom Johnson
episodes.lead: The killing of Tom Johnson was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Marshal Grant Cowan at Henryetta on or about 22 August 1905. It is known from a single sentence in the Guthrie Daily Leader, which gave no reason for the shooting.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Williams was the burning of a Black man by a crowd on the courthouse square at Sulphur Springs, Hopkins County, Texas, on August 11, 1905. Accused of attempting to assault a young white girl, he was taken from officers and burned after she identified him. The burning drew Black-press editorials and a later dispute over a Texas Negro Baptist convention's reported endorsement of it.

episodes.title: Portsmouth peace conference hotel bellhop incident
episodes.lead: The Portsmouth peace conference hotel bellhop incident was a confrontation in late August 1905 at the New Hampshire hotel housing the Russo-Japanese peace conference, in which a guest from Kentucky threatened to cut out the "black heart" of a Black bellhop and began to attack him. Four men pulled the man off, no injury was reported, and the New York Sun told the story as a joke about a near "race war."

episodes.title: Beating of W. M. Herdon
episodes.lead: The beating of W. M. Herdon was an assault on a Black man by a white man and a street crowd at First avenue S and Third street, apparently in Minneapolis, Minnesota, at about 1 a.m. on August 15, 1905. Herdon was severely beaten and then arrested by police for disorderly conduct, while no attacker is reported to have been held. The Minneapolis Journal's brief item framed the crowd as having helped "punish" a "colored man" for drawing a knife.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Will Horn
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Will Horn took place on August 17, 1905, when a mob was reported forming at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, to lynch Horn after his capture, and Governor Vardaman sent troops to take him away. Horn, a Black convict charged in the killing of J. G. Smith, the white man in charge of the city convict force, was carried under military guard to the Jackson jail, and no attack was made. Two other Black men had already been lynched at Hattiesburg over Smith's death, and Horn was later quoted as saying one of them was innocent.

episodes.title: Shooting of William Curtis
episodes.lead: The shooting of William Curtis was the killing of a Black laborer by Saratoga detective James Sullivan at Saratoga Springs, New York, on August 13, 1905, as officers tried to arrest him. Curtis was accused of beating the Rev. Bernard Schulte and his wife with a pipe at the St. Luke's Episcopal rectory in Mechanicsville the night before; both survived. The case ran nationally as a wire story that led with the assault and gave the police account of the shooting as fact; three Black weeklies reprinted it briefly.

episodes.title: York Dispatch lynching warning (1905)
episodes.lead: The York Dispatch lynching warning was a printed threat made in the summer of 1905 by the York Dispatch of York, Pennsylvania, against an unnamed Black man accused of striking a white woman who had stopped a dog fight. No attack on the man is reported, and the episode is known only from a brief item in the Montgomery Advertiser that quoted the Dispatch's warning and its closing word, "Lynching?"

episodes.title: Killing of Furgeson at Monroe, North Carolina
episodes.lead: The killing of Furgeson was the fatal shooting of a Black man at the railroad depot in Monroe, North Carolina, as he ran from H. J. Bivens, then constable of Monroe township, who was trying to arrest him for "beating a ride on the train." Bivens was tried for manslaughter in August 1905, and the trial ended in a mistrial when the jury failed to agree. The Monroe Journal called it the case "of most interest" in that term of court.
